:::{#thm-basis-unique}
#### Coefficients in a basis are unique

If $\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_k$ is a basis of a subspace $\mathcal{S}$
(@def-basis),
then every $\vecf{x} \in \mathcal{S}$ is a linear combination
$\vecf{x} = c_1 \vecf{a}_1 + \cdots + c_k \vecf{a}_k$
for exactly one list of numbers $c_1, \ldots, c_k$.

:::

::: proof

At least one such list exists,
because the basis spans $\mathcal{S}$ (@def-span).

Suppose two lists both work:

$$
c_1 \vecf{a}_1 + \cdots + c_k \vecf{a}_k
= \vecf{x}
= d_1 \vecf{a}_1 + \cdots + d_k \vecf{a}_k.
$$

Subtracting the right side from the left side gives

$$
\ba
\vzero
&= (c_1 \vecf{a}_1 + \cdots + c_k \vecf{a}_k)
 - (d_1 \vecf{a}_1 + \cdots + d_k \vecf{a}_k)
&& \text{(both combinations equal } \vecf{x} \text{)}
\\
&= (c_1 - d_1)\,\vecf{a}_1 + \cdots + (c_k - d_k)\,\vecf{a}_k
&& \text{(regroup, and distribute each } \vecf{a}_i \text{)}
\ea
$$

Because $\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_k$ are linearly independent
(@def-linearly-independent),
every coefficient $c_i - d_i$ is $0$,
so $c_i = d_i$ for each $i$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-basis-unique}
#### Coefficients of $(3, 5)$ in two bases

In the basis $(1, 0), (0, 1)$ of @exm-basis,
$(3, 5) = 3\,(1, 0) + 5\,(0, 1)$,
and no other coefficients work.
In the basis $(1, 0), (1, 1)$,
the formula in @exm-basis gives
$(3, 5) = (3 - 5)\,(1, 0) + 5\,(1, 1) = -2\,(1, 0) + 5\,(1, 1)$.
The same vector has different coefficients in different bases,
but within one basis its coefficients are unique.

The list $(1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)$ in @exm-not-basis spans $\reals^2$
but is not linearly independent,
and the coefficients of $(3, 5)$ are not unique:
$(3, 5) = 3\,(1, 0) + 5\,(0, 1) + 0\,(1, 1)
= 0\,(1, 0) + 2\,(0, 1) + 3\,(1, 1)$.

:::
